claims.sentence: A draft internet standard from Anthropic's Kevin Kelley, dated Oct 30, lets websites opt out of AI training with one robots.txt token, __usage_ai-training, which Microsoft says it will honor starting Feb 1, 2027, and Google aims to support in 2027.
In a preprint that is not yet peer-reviewed, a UIUC-led team reports that 90 of 99 results from 11 AI agent memory systems scored below naive RAG, a plain search over the raw conversation history.

Divyansh Agrawal's hobby project Qwenputer compiles a 32-bit RISC-V CPU into the Qwen3.5-4B model, and he reports it scored 97.5% on a 40-problem big-number multiplication set, against 55% for the stock model.
A draft standard dated Oct 30 defines one shared token for the job: `__usage_ai-training`.
The draft comes from Kevin Kelley of Anthropic. It is an individual proposal filed with the IETF, and the IETF's own tracker says it is "not endorsed by the IETF".
Anthropic says it has started implementing support, Google says it plans to support it, and Microsoft says it will honor it from Feb 1, 2027.
claims.changed: round 1: replaced 'have each said they will honor it'

claims.sentence: The draft adds "no new directive names and no new grammar," so older robots.txt readers simply skip it.
In the draft's example, `Disallow: /` paired with `Allow: /press-kit/` expresses a preference against training everywhere except the press kit, where it expresses a preference in favor.
claims.changed: round 1: 'means no training' replaced with preference wording

claims.sentence: "AI training" here means "using an asset to modify the learned parameters of a generative AI model".
A catch-all `User-Agent: *` group does not apply, so a site without the token has expressed no preference.
Anthropic "has already started implementing support for this draft," Kelley wrote on an IETF mailing list.
claims.changed: round 1: named Kelley as the message author, per factcheck evidence

claims.sentence: Google says the token lets owners "express their AI training preferences across multiple AI providers in a single step," and it aims to support it "in 2027".
"Starting February 1, 2027, Microsoft will honor the new preferences as it crawls," Microsoft says.
OpenAI will roll out support "in the coming months," according to a daily.dev summary of OpenAI's announcement.
AI Weekly and Vanessa Fox also report that OpenAI announced support.
claims.changed: round 1: added per coordinator; replaces the cut sentence 'We could not read OpenAI's own post' (N12)
claims.note: Supported by fact-check N11 evidence; no separate ledger claim for AI Weekly/Fox on OpenAI.

claims.sentence: "Training and grounding are independent preferences," Microsoft says.
Grounding is when an AI assistant pulls in web pages to answer a question.
Microsoft says neither setting changes whether a site can appear in regular Bing results, subject to its normal crawl and indexing requirements.
claims.changed: round 1: added the qualifier the fact-checker suggested

claims.sentence: Google says Google-Extended, its own AI-training token, "does not impact a site's inclusion in Google Search".
"This policy token is not a directive for crawling behavior," the draft says.
Nothing forces anyone to obey, and an editor's note on AI Weekly's alert says it has "no enforcement teeth".
claims.changed: round 1: attributed to AI Weekly's editor's note

claims.sentence: Private deals between a site and an AI company can also override it.
The signal "says nothing about web search, AI answers, or user-triggered requests," Vanessa Fox writes.

Nate Hake of Travel Lemming, in posts on X shown by Search Engine Roundtable, said the draft "basically exempts the preferences from applying to anything a user does." He added that "it's not actually done at the ietf level -- and some significant areas of dispute remain".
claims.changed: round 1: described as X posts, not interview comments

claims.sentence: Unless a site names Google-Extended itself, Google plans to read a token opt-out "as if the publisher had disallowed Google-Extended".
Google says sites that "specifically allow Google-Extended are eligible to appear" in grounded answers in Gemini Apps.
claims.changed: round 1: removed 'only'

claims.sentence: Our reading, not Google's statement: a site that opts out with the new token and does not name Google-Extended would not count as specifically allowing it, so it could lose eligibility for those answers.

claims.sentence: Purpose-built memory systems for AI agents often do worse than simply searching the raw conversation history, a team led from UIUC reports.
"We find many dedicated memory systems underperform naive RAG in many cases, indicating a negative net value," the authors write.
The preprint was posted to arXiv on Oct 25 and is not yet peer-reviewed.
It drew 157 upvotes after Hugging Face Daily Papers listed it on Oct 28.
A memory system rewrites an agent's past chats into facts, summaries or graphs ... Naive RAG ... cuts the raw history into chunks, searches them and hands the best matches to the model.
The paper splits a memory system's value into a "memory benefit" and a "memory tax".
Memory "does solve some queries RAG misses," the authors write, "while losing others that RAG already solves".
90 of 99. That many results, from 11 memory systems on 3 benchmarks with 3 AI models, fell below the paper's stronger, two-round RAG baseline, according to the project page.

claims.sentence: The models were Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.6-27B and GPT-5.6 Luna at a low reasoning setting.

That is what a basic RAG-Hybrid baseline reaches on some of the memory benchmarks the authors checked, and a simple keyword matcher tops 50% on some.

Divyansh Agrawal built a working computer processor inside Qwen3.5-4B, a small open language model, using the model's own Gated DeltaNet layers as RAM.
His write-up is dated Oct 22.
A Hacker News post about it from Oct 29 shows 695 points.
